A recent social media post claims that the Pfizer vaccine causes "long-term neurological disorders." This statement has sparked concerns among the public about vaccine safety and potential side effects. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is essential to examine the available scientific evidence, regulatory guidance, and context surrounding the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine.

The Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine, also known as BNT162b2 or Comirnaty, was one of the first vaccines authorized for emergency use during the COVID-19 pandemic. It uses messenger RNA (mRNA) technology to instruct cells to produce a harmless piece of the coronavirus spike protein, prompting an immune response. Since its introduction, hundreds of millions of doses have been administered worldwide.

The claim that the Pfizer vaccine causes "long-term neurological disorders" suggests that recipients are at significant risk of developing persistent or delayed-onset nervous system diseases. Neurological disorders can include a range of conditions, such as Guillain-Barré Syndrome, multiple sclerosis, seizures, or chronic neuropathies. Such a claim, if substantiated, would have serious implications for public health policy and vaccine confidence.

According to clinical trial data and ongoing safety monitoring by regulatory agencies, the vast majority of reported side effects from the Pfizer vaccine are mild and temporary, such as soreness at the injection site, fatigue, headache, and mild fever. While rare adverse events, including some neurological symptoms, have been reported following vaccination, these are extremely uncommon. The most notable neurological side effect identified in rare cases has been myocarditis (heart inflammation), particularly among young males, but this is not classified as a primary neurological disorder.

Global health authorities, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the European Medicines Agency, have conducted ongoing surveillance of vaccine safety. These agencies require vaccine manufacturers to report adverse events and conduct long-term follow-up studies. To date, there is no credible scientific evidence demonstrating that the Pfizer vaccine causes widespread or increased risk of long-term neurological disorders among recipients.

It is important to note that neurological symptoms can also be triggered by a variety of causes, including viral infections like COVID-19 itself. In fact, COVID-19 infection has been associated with a higher risk of neurological complications than vaccination. When rare neurological events have occurred after vaccination, investigations have generally found no causal link or have determined the risk to be extremely low—much lower than the risks associated with the disease the vaccine is designed to prevent.

In conclusion, while ongoing monitoring for rare side effects continues, the claim that the Pfizer vaccine causes "long-term neurological disorders" is not supported by current scientific evidence or safety data. Health authorities worldwide continue to recommend the Pfizer vaccine as a safe and effective measure to prevent COVID-19 and its potentially severe complications. As with any medical intervention, individuals with specific concerns should consult their healthcare providers for personalized information.

A recent social media post claims, “After the COVID-19 vaccine, people become infected,” suggesting that the vaccines may not prevent infection or could even be responsible for causing infections. To assess the accuracy of this statement, it is important to examine how COVID-19 vaccines work, what is known about breakthrough infections, and the broader context of vaccine efficacy.

COVID-19 vaccines, including those developed by Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna, and Johnson & Johnson, were authorized after rigorous clinical trials demonstrated that they are highly effective at preventing severe illness, hospitalization, and death caused by the coronavirus. However, no vaccine is 100% effective at preventing infection. From the beginning of the vaccine rollout, public health officials have communicated that while the vaccines drastically reduce the risk of severe outcomes, some vaccinated individuals may still contract COVID-19 in what are known as “breakthrough infections.”

Breakthrough cases are expected with any vaccine. In the case of COVID-19, these infections occur when a fully vaccinated person is exposed to and infected by the virus. The frequency of breakthrough infections has fluctuated, especially with the emergence of highly transmissible variants such as Delta and Omicron. These variants have shown an increased ability to partially evade the immune protection conferred by vaccination.

Importantly, the core purpose of the COVID-19 vaccines is to prime the immune system so that if an individual is exposed to the virus, their body can mount a swift and effective response. This reduces the chances of severe symptoms and long-term complications. Data from real-world studies consistently show that vaccinated individuals are much less likely to experience severe illness or require hospitalization compared to those who are unvaccinated.

The claim that “after the COVID-19 vaccine, people become infected” is partially accurate but lacks critical context. Vaccines do not guarantee total immunity from infection, but they significantly decrease the likelihood of severe outcomes. Additionally, there is no evidence that the vaccines themselves cause COVID-19 infection. The vaccines do not contain live virus capable of causing disease; rather, they use inactivated virus, viral vectors, or messenger RNA to instruct the body to recognize and fight the virus if exposed in the future.

In summary, it is true that some people may become infected with COVID-19 after being vaccinated, but these cases are generally less severe, and the overall risk of infection and transmission is lower among vaccinated populations. The vaccines remain a vital tool in reducing the burden of COVID-19, especially in preventing hospitalizations and deaths. The claim, when stripped of context, may mislead readers into doubting the effectiveness and safety of COVID-19 vaccines, which continue to play a crucial role in managing the pandemic.

ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို ရရှိသော နောက်ဆုံးအခြေအနေများသည် ကိုးကားတစ်ခုခုကို ဖြစ်ပေါ်စေနိုင်သည်။ ကိုဗစ်-၁၉ ကူးစက်ရောဂါများတွင် ကူးစက်ရောဂါများသည် ကိုးကားရရှိသူများသည် ပိုးကောင်းကို အကြိမ်အကြာ ကူးစက်ခံရပြီး ကူးစက်ရောဂါဖြစ်ပွားသည့်အခြေအနေဖြစ်ပါသည်။ ကူးစက်ရောဂါဖြစ်ပွားမှုများသည် အထူးသဖြင့် အထူးပြောင်းလဲမှုများကို ပိုမိုပြောင်းလဲစေသော ကူးစက်မှုများကို လေ့လာရန်အတွက် ကူးစက်မှုများကို ပြောင်းလဲနေပါသည်။ ဤပြောင်းလဲမှုများသည် ကူးစက်မှုကို ကာကွယ်ပေးခဲ့သည့် ကိုးကားများကို အစားထိုးနိုင်စေသည့် အခြေအနေများကို ပိုမိုကျော်လွန်နိုင်သည်ဟု ဆိုလိုပါသည်။

အထူးသဖြင့် ကိုဗစ်-၁၉ ကိုးကားများ၏ အဓိကရည်ရွယ်ချက်မှာ ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို ရရှိပြီးနောက် ကိုးကားများကို ခွဲခြားပြီး အရေးကြီးသော အခြေအနေများကို မြန်မြန်ဆန်ဆန် အားဖြင့် ဖြေရှင်းနိုင်ရန် ခန္တာကိုယ်အား ပိုမိုကောင်းမွန်စေရန် ဖြစ်သည်။ အခြေအနေများကို ကူးစက်ခြင်းမှ ကာကွယ်ပေးသော အခြေအနေများကို လျော့နည်းစေသည်။ အမှန်တကယ် လေ့လာမှုများအရ ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို ရရှိပြီးနောက် ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို ကာကွယ်ပေးသော ကိုးကားရရှိသူများသည် ကူးစက်မှုကို ရရှိသည့် အခြေအနေများနှင့် နှိုင်းယှဉ်ပါက ကူးစက်မှုကို ရရှိနိုင်သည့် အခြေအနေများကို ပိုမိုနည်းပါးစေသည်။

"ကိုဗစ်-၁၉ ကိုးကားရရှိပြီးနောက် လူတိုင်းကူးစက်နေကြသည်" ဟု ပြောဆိုထားသည့် ဆိုင်ကြောင်းအကြောင်းကို အစိတ်အပိုင်းအလုံးအစုံကို ဖော်ပြထားသည့်အပြင် အထူးအကြောင်းအရာများ မရှိပါ။ ကိုးကားများသည် ကူးစက်မှုကို တားဆီးနိုင်သည့် အထူးအကြောင်းအရာများကို အာမခံပေးနိုင်သည်။ သို့သော် ကိုးကားများသည် ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို ဖြစ်ပွားစေသည့် အခြေအနေများကို ဖြစ်ပွားစေသည့် အခြေအနေများကို အလွန်အများအပြား ကျဆင်းစေသည်။ ကိုးကားများသည် ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို ဖြစ်ပွားစေသည့် အခြေအနေများကို ကာကွယ်နိုင်သည့် ပိုးကောင်းများကို သို့မဟုတ် ပိုးကောင်းကို အကြိမ်အကြာ ဖြစ်ပွားစေသည့် ပိုးကောင်းများကို ပါဝင်ပေးသည့် မိုးကားရေးများကို အသုံးပြုပြီး နောင်တွင် ပိုးကောင်းကို ရရှိပြီးနောက် ခွဲခြားသိမ်းဆည်းနိုင်သည့် အခြေအနေများကို ပြုလုပ်သည်။

အကျိုးအများအပြားအတွက် ကိုဗစ်-၁၉ ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို ကာကွယ်ပေးသည့် ကိုးကားများကို ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို ရရှိပြီးနောက် ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို ရရှိနိုင်သည့် အခြေအနေများကို အားကောင်းစေပြီး ပိုးကောင်းကို ကူးစက်ခြင်းမှ ကာကွယ်ပေးသည့် အခြေအနေများကို လျော့နည်းစေသည့် အခြေအနေများကို ကျွန်းဆီးခဲ့ပါသည်။ ကိုးကားများကို အားလုံးကို အားကောင်းစေပြီး ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို ကာကွယ်ပေးသည့် ကိုးကားများသည် ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို အားကောင်းစေပြီး ပိုးကောင်းကို ကူးစက်ခြင်းမှ ကာကွယ်ပေးသည့် အခြေအနေများကို အလွန်အများအပြား ကျဆင်းစေသည်။ ကိုးကားများကို အားလုံးကို အားကောင်းစေပြီး ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို ကာကွယ်ပေးသည့် ကိုးကားများကို နှိုးဆော်နိုင်သည့် အခြေအနေများကို ထုတ်ပြန်ပေးသည့် အခြေအနေများကို မှားယွင်းစေနိုင်သည့် အခြေအနေများကို အထူးသဖြင့် အကြံပြုသည့် ကိုးကားများကို အလွန်အများအပြား ကျဆင်းစေသည်။ ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို ကာကွယ်ပေးသည့် ကိုးကားများသည် ပိုးကောင်းကို ကူးစက်ခြင်းမှ ကာကွယ်ပေးသည့် ကိုးကားများကို ဆက်လက်ကာကွယ်နေသည့် အခြေအနေများကို အလွန်အများအပြား ကျဆင်းစေသည်။

Claims have circulated on social media asserting that Ukraine has canceled its mask regime, lifting previous requirements for citizens to wear face masks in public spaces. This article examines the validity of these claims, provides context about Ukraine’s COVID-19 response, and clarifies the current status of mask mandates in the country.

As the COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020, Ukraine, like many other countries, implemented a series of public health measures to curb the virus’s transmission. Among these measures was the introduction of a mask mandate, requiring citizens to wear face coverings in indoor public places, on public transportation, and in crowded outdoor spaces. Compliance with mask-wearing became widespread, enforced by local authorities and public health officials.

Throughout 2021 and 2022, Ukraine adjusted its COVID-19 restrictions in response to changing infection rates, vaccination progress, and the emergence of new variants. The government adopted a flexible, region-based approach, classifying regions by “green,” “yellow,” “orange,” and “red” zones, with restrictions—including mask mandates—varying accordingly. Mask requirements remained stricter in “red” zones experiencing surges in cases.

In 2022, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine shifted national priorities. While the war created new public health challenges, it also limited the ability of authorities to enforce COVID-19 regulations. Evacuations, sheltering in crowded spaces, and disruptions to healthcare infrastructure affected both the spread of the virus and the enforcement of mitigation measures, including mask-wearing.

By 2023 and into 2024, many countries began easing pandemic-era restrictions as vaccination rates increased and the severity of COVID-19 cases declined. In Ukraine, the Ministry of Health reviewed the necessity of ongoing public health restrictions, including mask mandates. In the spring of 2023, the Ukrainian government announced the cancellation of its nationwide mask regime, lifting the requirement to wear face masks in most public spaces. This decision was based on improved epidemiological indicators and the pressing challenges posed by the ongoing war. As of early 2024, Ukraine no longer mandates masks in public spaces at the national level. However, authorities continue to recommend mask-wearing in healthcare settings, for individuals with respiratory symptoms, and in crowded or poorly ventilated environments.

It is important to note that while the national mask mandate has been lifted, local or institutional requirements may still apply. Hospitals, clinics, and some public transport operators may retain mask policies for the safety of vulnerable populations. Additionally, the Ministry of Health reserves the right to reinstate stricter measures if a significant COVID-19 outbreak occurs.

In summary, the core claim that “Ukraine canceled mask regime” is accurate. The Ukrainian government has officially lifted the national requirement for citizens to wear masks in public spaces, reflecting a transition to living with COVID-19 as an endemic illness. Nonetheless, public health recommendations and some localized requirements remain, underscoring the importance of personal responsibility in preventing the spread of respiratory infections.

ਜਦੋਂ ਕੋਰੋਨਾ ਵਾਇਰਸ ਦੇ ਮਹਾਮਾਰੀ ਦੇ ਵਿਸ਼ਵ ਵਿੱਚ ਫੈਲਣ ਦੇ ਸ਼ੁਰੂਆਤੀ ਵਰ੍ਹੇਵਾਂ ਵਿੱਚ, ਯੂਕਰੇਨ, ਬਹੁਤ ਸਾਰੇ ਦੇਸ਼ਾਂ ਵਰਗੇ, ਵਾਇਰਸ ਦੇ ਫੈਲਣ ਨੂੰ ਰੋਕਣ ਲਈ ਇੱਕ ਸੰਖੇਪ ਸਿਹਤ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਨਿਕ ਪ੍ਰਬੰਧ ਦੀ ਸਥਾਪਨਾ ਕੀਤੀ ਗਈ ਸੀ। ਇਸ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਨਿਕ ਪ੍ਰਬੰਧ ਦੇ ਵਿੱਚੋਂ ਇੱਕ ਮਾਸਕ ਨੀਤੀ ਸ਼ਾਮਲ ਸੀ, ਜਿਸ ਦੇ ਅਧੀਨ ਨਾਗਰਿਕਾਂ ਨੂੰ ਬਾਹਰੀ ਜੰਗਲੀ ਸਪੇਸ ਵਿੱਚ ਭੰਡਾਰਾਂ ਵਾਲੇ ਸਥਾਨਾਂ, ਸਾਂਝੇ ਸਾਂਝੇ ਸ਼ਹਿਰੀ ਪਰਿਵਹਨ ਅਤੇ ਵਿਸ਼ਾਲ ਬਾਹਰੀ ਸਪੇਸ ਵਿੱਚ ਚਿਹਰੇ ਦੀ ਕਵਰੇਜ ਪਹਿਨਣ ਲਈ ਕਿਹਾ ਗਿਆ ਸੀ। ਮਾਸਕ ਪਹਿਨਣ ਦੀ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਨਿਕ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਨ ਵਿੱਚ ਸਥਾਨਕ ਅਧਿਕਾਰੀਆਂ ਅਤੇ ਸਿਹਤ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਨਿਕ ਅਧਿਕਾਰੀਆਂ ਦੁਆਰਾ ਵਿਸ਼ਵਸ਼ਾਲੀ ਹੋ ਗਈ ਸੀ।

2022 ਵਿੱਚ, ਰੂਸ ਦੀ ਯੂਕਰੇਨ ਵਿੱਚ ਪੂਰਨ ਅਤੇ ਜ਼ੋਰੀ ਹਮਲਾ ਦੇ ਨਤੀਜੇ ਵਜੋਂ, ਰਾਸ਼ਟਰੀ ਮਾਨ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਨ ਦੀ ਸਥਿਤੀ ਬਦਲ ਗਈ। ਹਾਲਾਂਕਿ ਯੂਗ ਨੇ ਨਵੇਂ ਸਿਹਤ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਨਿਕ ਚੁਣੌਤੀਆਂ ਪੈਦਾ ਕੀਤੀਆਂ, ਇਸ ਨੇ ਅਧਿਕਾਰੀਆਂ ਦੇ ਕੋਰੋਨਾ ਵਾਇਰਸ ਦੇ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਨਿਕ ਨਿਯਮਾਂ ਦੀ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਨ ਦੀ ਸਮਰੂਪਤਾ ਨੂੰ ਸੀਮਿਤ ਕਰ ਦਿੱਤਾ। ਵਿਸ਼ਵਾਸ ਕਰਨ, ਭੰਡਾਰਾਂ ਵਿੱਚ ਸੰਭਾਲਣ, ਅਤੇ ਸਿਹਤ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਨਿਕ ਸੰਸਥਾਵਾਂ ਦੀ ਖ਼ਲਾਫ਼ ਅਸਥਿਰਤਾ ਨੇ ਵਾਇਰਸ ਦੇ ਫੈਲਣ ਅਤੇ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਨਿਕ ਨਿਯਮਾਂ ਦੀ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਨ ਦੀ ਸਮਰੂਪਤਾ ਨੂੰ ਪ੍ਰਭਾਵਿਤ ਕੀਤਾ।

A claim circulating on social media states that “60% of all new COVID-19 cases are among people who have been vaccinated.” This assertion has generated concern and confusion, prompting questions about the effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccines and the current dynamics of the pandemic. A careful examination of the available data and public health context is necessary to accurately assess the validity of this claim.

To begin, it is important to understand how COVID-19 vaccines work and what breakthrough cases are. Vaccines against COVID-19 are highly effective at preventing severe illness, hospitalization, and death. However, no vaccine is 100% effective at preventing infection. Breakthrough infections—cases where fully vaccinated individuals contract the virus—do occur, especially as immunity may wane over time and as new variants emerge. The key point is that, while vaccines reduce the risk of infection, their primary benefit is in reducing the severity of disease.

The claim that 60% of all new COVID-19 cases are among vaccinated individuals is misleading without important context. As vaccination rates increase within a population, the proportion of cases among vaccinated individuals will also rise. This is a statistical phenomenon known as the “base rate effect.” If a very high percentage of the population is vaccinated, then even a highly effective vaccine will result in some cases among vaccinated people, simply because there are fewer unvaccinated people remaining.

For example, if 90% of a population is vaccinated and 10% are unvaccinated, and if the vaccine is 90% effective at preventing infection, there will still be some cases among the vaccinated group. Because such a large portion of the population is vaccinated, the absolute number of cases in this group can appear high, even if the unvaccinated are at significantly greater risk on an individual basis.

Public health data from various countries have, at times, shown that a majority of new COVID-19 cases are among vaccinated people, particularly in highly vaccinated countries. However, these figures must be interpreted with caution. The risk of infection, hospitalization, and death remains much higher among the unvaccinated. Vaccinated individuals who do contract the virus are, on average, much less likely to experience severe outcomes.

Additionally, the percentage of cases among vaccinated individuals can be influenced by factors such as the time since vaccination, the emergence of new variants, and the implementation of booster campaigns. It is also important to note that case counts can fluctuate based on the level of community transmission and testing practices.

In summary, while it is sometimes true that a significant proportion of new COVID-19 cases occur among vaccinated individuals, this does not mean that vaccines are ineffective. Rather, it reflects the high level of vaccination coverage and the statistical realities of a large vaccinated population. Vaccines continue to provide strong protection against severe disease and remain a crucial tool in managing the pandemic. The claim, when presented without context, risks misrepresenting the effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccination.

সামাজিক মাধ্যমত প্রচারিত একটা দাবি আছে যে, "সকল নতুন কোভিড-১৯ কেসের ৬০% বাক্সিন কৰা মানুহৰ মাজত হয়।" এই দাবিটো চিন্তা আৰু বিষয়া সংকোচন সৃষ্টি কৰিছে আৰু কোভিড-১৯ ভাইক্সিনৰ কাৰ্যকাৰিতা আৰু বৰ্তমান মহামারীৰ সামগ্রিক দৃশ্য সম্পৰ্কত প্ৰশ্ন উঠিছে। পৰিস্থিতি আৰু সামাজিক আৰোগ্য তথ্য সম্পৰ্কত এটা সত্য পৰীক্ষা কৰিব প্ৰয়োজন যাতে এই দাবিৰ সত্যতা সঠিকভাবে পৰিমাপ কৰিব পাৰি।

প্ৰথমতে, কোভিড-১৯ ভাইক্সিনৰ কামকৰ্ম আৰু ব্রেকথ্ৰু কেছ বুজিব প্ৰয়োজন। কোভিড-১৯ বিপত্তিৰ বিপত্তিৰ মুখৰ পৰা মৃত্যু আৰু আস্পতালৰ প্ৰবেশ পৰিহাৰ কৰিবলৈ ভাইক্সিন অত্যন্ত কাৰ্যকৰী হয়। কিন্তু কোনো ভাইক্সিন পৰিপূৰ্ণ পৰিমাণে আক্রান্ত হোৱা পৰা পৰা পৰিহাৰ কৰিব নোৱাৰে। ব্রেকথ্ৰু কেছ বুলি কোৱা হয় যে সম্পূৰ্ণ ভাইক্সিন কৰা মানুহে ভাইৰাছ আক্রান্ত হয়, বিশেষত যেতিয়া পৰিপূৰ্ণতা কম হয় আৰু নতুন বিষাক উদ্ভৱ হয়। প্ৰধান বিষয় হৈছে যে, ভাইক্সিন আক্রান্ত হোৱাৰ জৰিত কম কৰিব পাৰে কিন্তু এই ভাইক্সিনৰ মুখ্য উপকাৰিতা হৈছে বিষাক বিপত্তিৰ গুৰুত্বপূৰ্ণ ফলাফল কম কৰিব।

ভাইক্সিন কৰা মানুহৰ মাজত সকলো নতুন কোভিড-১৯ কেছৰ ৬০% হোৱা দাবি কোনো গুৰুত্বপূৰ্ণ সংকেত বিহীন হৈ ভুল বুজায়। যেতিয়া ভাইক্সিন কৰা মানুহৰ সংখ্যা এটা জনগণৰ মাজত বৃদ্ধি পায়, তেতিয়া ভাইক্সিন কৰা মানুহৰ মাজত কেছৰ পৰিমাণ আৰু বৃদ্ধি পাব। এই এটা স্ট্যাটিস্টিক ঘটনা যাক "বেজ চৰ ইফেক্ট" বুলি কোৱা হয়। যদি জনগণৰ অতি উচ্চ পৰিমাণ ভাইক্সিন কৰা হয়, তেতিয়া এটা সম্পূৰ্ণ কাৰ্যকৰী ভাইক্সিনৰ ফলত ভাইক্সিন কৰা মানুহৰ মাজত কেছ হৈ থাকিব কাৰণ বাকী ভাইক্সিন নকৰা মানুহৰ সংখ্যা কম হৈছে।

যেনে এটা উদাহৰণ, যদি জনগণৰ ৯০% ভাইক্সিন কৰা হয় আৰু ১০% ভাইক্সিন নকৰা হয় আৰু ভাইক্সিন কৰা মানুহৰ পৰা আক্রান্ত হোৱা পৰা পৰিহাৰ কৰিব পৰা সম্ভাবনা ৯০% হয়, তেতিয়াও ভাইক্সিন কৰা মানুহৰ মাজত কেছ হব। কাৰণ জনগণৰ অতি বৃহৎ অংশ ভাইক্সিন কৰা হৈছে, তেতিয়া এই গৰিষ্ঠ সংখ্যা ভাইক্সিন কৰা মানুহৰ মাজত দেখুৱাই থাকিব যদিও ভাইক্সিন নকৰা মানুহ বিপত্তিৰ বিষয়ে বিশেষ কৰি বেছি বেয়া সম্ভাবনা থাকিব।

বিভিন্ন দেশৰ সামাজিক আৰোগ্য তথ্য আৰু বিশেষত উচ্চ ভাইক্সিন কৰা দেশৰ মাজত এটা পৰিস্থিতি দেখা গৈছে যে বেছি ভাইক্সিন কৰা মানুহৰ মাজত সকলো নতুন কোভিড-১৯ কেছ হয়। কিন্তু এই সংখ্যা সাবধানে ব্যাখ্যা কৰিব লাগে। ভাইক্সিন নকৰা মানুহৰ পৰা আক্রান্ত হোৱা, আস্পতাল পৰিহাৰ আৰু মৃত্যুৰ সম্ভাবনা বেছি হয়। ভাইক্সিন কৰা মানুহ যিসকল ভাইৰাছ আক্রান্ত হয়, তেওঁলোকৰ বিপত্তিৰ গুৰুত্বপূৰ্ণ ফলাফল কম সম্ভাবনা থাকে।

সৈতে, ভাইক্সিন কৰা মানুহৰ মাজত কেছৰ পৰিমাণ সময়ৰ পৰিৱৰ্তন, নতুন বিষাক উদ্ভৱ হোৱা আৰু বুস্টাৰ ক্যাম্পেইন প্ৰয়োগ আদি কাৰণৰ পৰিবৰ্তন হোৱা পাৰে। আৰু সামাজিক প্ৰবাহ আৰু পৰীক্ষা পদ্ধতিৰ পৰিবৰ্তন আৰু কেছ সংখ্যাৰ পৰিবৰ্তন কাৰণে এই পৰিমাণ পৰিৱৰ্তন হোৱা পাৰে।

সংক্ষেপত, ভাইক্সিন কৰা মানুহৰ মাজত সকলো নতুন কোভিড-১৯ কেছৰ এটা বৃহৎ অংশ হৈছে এটা সত্য হৈছে, কিন্তু এই কথাটো ভাইক্সিন অকাৰ্যকৰী হৈছে নহয়। বিপরীতে এটা সত্য হৈছে যে ভাইক্সিন কৰা মানুহৰ সংখ্যা উচ্চ আৰু বৃহৎ ভাইক্সিন কৰা জনগণৰ স্ট্যাটিস্টিক সত্যতা। ভাইক্সিন অকার্যকৰী হৈ নাই আৰু এই মহামারী পৰিচালনাৰ জন্য এটা গুৰুত্বপূৰ্ণ উপাদান। দাবি যদি কোনো সংকেত বিহীন হৈ প্ৰকাশ কৰা হয়, তেতিয়া কোভিড-১৯ ভাইক্সিন কৰাৰ কাৰ্যকারিতা ভুল বুজাই থাকিব।

The claim that "vaccination passports are introduced for the management and control of people" has circulated widely on social media, especially during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. To evaluate the accuracy of this statement, it is important to examine what vaccination passports are, why they were implemented, and whether their primary purpose is public health or social control.

Vaccination passports, also known as vaccine certificates or digital health passes, are documents—physical or digital—that certify an individual’s vaccination status. They became particularly prominent during the COVID-19 pandemic as governments and organizations sought ways to safely reopen borders, workplaces, and public events while reducing the risk of disease transmission.

The concept of requiring proof of immunization for travel or participation in certain activities is not new. For decades, travelers to some countries have been required to present International Certificates of Vaccination, such as the “yellow card” for yellow fever. With COVID-19, the scale of implementation expanded, given the global impact of the disease and the urgent need to resume social and economic activities.

The primary stated purpose of vaccination passports is public health. By verifying that individuals have been vaccinated against COVID-19, or occasionally tested negative for the virus, these documents are intended to reduce the risk of outbreaks in crowded or high-risk settings. Many countries introduced such measures to allow safer international travel, access to large gatherings, or entry into public venues like restaurants, gyms, and theaters.

However, concerns about privacy, equity, and government overreach have been voiced by critics. Some fear that vaccination passports could be used to discriminate against those who are unvaccinated, either by choice or due to lack of access, or that they could set a precedent for broader surveillance and control measures. These concerns often fuel claims that the true purpose of vaccination passports is to manage or control people, rather than to protect public health.

An examination of government policies and public statements, however, indicates that the primary rationale for vaccination passports has been to mitigate transmission and enable a return to normalcy. The requirements have generally been temporary and tied specifically to the pandemic context. In many regions, such requirements have been lifted or relaxed as vaccination rates increased and the public health threat diminished.

There is limited evidence to support the claim that vaccination passports were introduced with the primary goal of controlling populations beyond the context of public health. While the implementation of any health-related policy requires oversight and enforcement, the introduction of vaccination passports has largely been framed as a response to an unprecedented global health crisis, not as an instrument of population management or social control.

In summary, while it is understandable that some may be concerned about the broader implications of vaccination passports, the available evidence indicates that their primary purpose has been public health protection during the COVID-19 pandemic. The assertion that they were introduced chiefly for the management and control of people overstates the intent and ignores the context in which these measures were adopted.

Vaccination passports, also known as vaccine certificates or digital health passes, are documents—physical or digital—that certify an individual's vaccination status. They became particularly prominent during the COVID-19 pandemic as governments and organizations sought ways to safely reopen borders, workplaces, and public events while reducing the risk of disease transmission.

The concept of requiring proof of immunization for travel or participation in certain activities is not new. For decades, travelers to some countries have been required to present International Certificates of Vaccination, such as the “yellow card” for yellow fever. With COVID-19, the scale of implementation expanded, given the global impact of the disease and the urgent need to resume social and economic activities.

The primary stated purpose of vaccination passports is public health. By verifying that individuals have been vaccinated against COVID-19, or occasionally tested negative for the virus, these documents are intended to reduce the risk of outbreaks in crowded or high-risk settings. Many countries introduced such measures to allow safer international travel, access to large gatherings, or entry into public venues like restaurants, gyms, and theaters.

However, concerns about privacy, equity, and government overreach have been voiced by critics. Some fear that vaccination passports could be used to discriminate against those who are unvaccinated, either by choice or due to lack of access, or that they could set a precedent for broader surveillance and control measures. These concerns often fuel claims that the true purpose of vaccination passports is to manage or control people, rather than to protect public health.

An examination of government policies and public statements, however, indicates that the primary rationale for vaccination passports has been to mitigate transmission and enable a return to normalcy. The requirements have generally been temporary and tied specifically to the pandemic context. In many regions, such requirements have been lifted or relaxed as vaccination rates increased and the public health threat diminished.

There is limited evidence to support the claim that vaccination passports were introduced with the primary goal of controlling populations beyond the context of public health. While the implementation of any health-related policy requires oversight and enforcement, the introduction of vaccination passports has largely been framed as a response to an unprecedented global health crisis, not as an instrument of population management or social control.

In summary, while it is understandable that some may be concerned about the broader implications of vaccination passports, the available evidence indicates that their primary purpose has been public health protection during the COVID-19 pandemic. The assertion that they were introduced chiefly for the management and control of people overstates the intent and ignores the context in which these measures were adopted.

A claim circulating on social media asserts that the number of miscarriages in the UK increased by 366% as a result of vaccination against COVID-19. This statement has sparked alarm and concern, particularly among those considering COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is essential to examine the available evidence, scientific studies, and official health data.

First, it is important to understand the context of COVID-19 vaccination in the UK. The UK’s vaccination program began in December 2020, and by early 2021, COVID-19 vaccines had become widely available, including to pregnant women. The Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) recommended vaccination for pregnant women following data suggesting the risks of COVID-19 infection during pregnancy could be significant, especially for those with underlying health conditions.

The claim of a 366% increase in miscarriages due to COVID-19 vaccination appears to originate from misinterpretation or selective use of data. Often, such claims are based on reports submitted to the UK’s Yellow Card scheme, which is a system for collecting and monitoring suspected side effects of medicines and vaccines. However, these reports alone cannot establish causation. Anyone can submit a Yellow Card report, and the reports do not verify that the vaccine caused the reported event. Furthermore, the number of reports may reflect increased surveillance and awareness, rather than an actual increase in adverse outcomes.

Major studies and reviews conducted in the UK and internationally have not found evidence to support a link between COVID-19 vaccines and increased risk of miscarriage. Health agencies have continuously monitored pregnancy outcomes, comparing miscarriage rates before and after the introduction of COVID-19 vaccines. The findings consistently show that miscarriage rates remain within the expected range for the general population. In the UK, the background rate of miscarriage—pregnancy loss before 20 weeks—is estimated at around 1 in 4 pregnancies. Analysis of vaccinated and unvaccinated populations does not demonstrate a spike or sustained increase in miscarriage rates following vaccination rollout.

Additionally, scientific studies have shown that COVID-19 infection itself is associated with higher risks of complications during pregnancy, including preterm birth and severe illness. Vaccination has been shown to reduce these risks, offering protection to both pregnant individuals and their babies.

The claim of a 366% increase is not supported by credible data or peer-reviewed research. It appears to rely on misinterpretation of voluntary reporting systems, without consideration for the limitations of such data or the broader scientific evidence. Health authorities, including the UK’s Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) and the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, endorse the safety of COVID-19 vaccines in pregnancy based on extensive monitoring and research.

In summary, there is no substantiated evidence that COVID-19 vaccination has caused a 366% increase in miscarriages in the UK. Misinformation around this topic can cause unnecessary fear and may discourage people from receiving safe and effective vaccines. The current scientific consensus is that COVID-19 vaccines are safe for pregnant women and do not increase the risk of miscarriage.

A recent social media post claims that more Ukrainians have been ill with influenza than with COVID-19, prompting confusion and debate online. To assess the accuracy of this statement, it is essential to examine both the historical context of influenza in Ukraine as well as the impact and official data for COVID-19.

**Background: Influenza and COVID-19 in Ukraine**  
Ukraine, like many countries in Eastern Europe, has regularly faced seasonal outbreaks of influenza. In the years before the COVID-19 pandemic, it was not uncommon for millions of Ukrainians to contract influenza or similar respiratory illnesses during the annual flu season. Public health campaigns have long encouraged vaccination and preventive measures to mitigate the impact.

With the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020, Ukraine, along with the rest of the world, encountered a new and highly transmissible viral threat. COVID-19 led to waves of infection, hospitalizations, and significant mortality. The Ukrainian government, health authorities, and international organizations mobilized to track and respond to the evolving situation.

**Evaluating the Claim: Cumulative Case Numbers**  
To fact-check the claim, it is necessary to compare cumulative case numbers of influenza and COVID-19 in Ukraine.

For influenza, estimates from pre-pandemic years indicate that annual seasonal flu epidemics could infect between 3 to 7 million Ukrainians per year, depending on the severity of the season. For example, in the 2018-2019 and 2019-2020 flu seasons, official health data suggested that approximately 4 to 6 million cases of influenza and acute respiratory viral infections (ARVI) were registered each year. These numbers, however, include both laboratory-confirmed influenza cases and broader ARVI, which encompasses a range of respiratory viruses.

In contrast, as of mid-2023, Ukraine reported just over 5.5 million confirmed cases of COVID-19 since the pandemic began. These numbers are based on official testing and reporting, though actual infections may be higher due to underreporting, limited testing, or asymptomatic cases.

**Context and Analysis**  
Comparing the two illnesses is not straightforward. Influenza case numbers in Ukraine are annual and can accumulate rapidly, sometimes outpacing the total official COVID-19 case count over a single year. However, the data for influenza often includes all "acute respiratory viral infections," not just laboratory-confirmed flu cases, potentially inflating the numbers compared to confirmed COVID-19 cases.

COVID-19, on the other hand, presented a unique and unprecedented public health challenge. Despite lower official case numbers compared to some annual flu seasons, COVID-19 resulted in a significantly higher mortality rate and greater strain on the health system than seasonal flu.

**Conclusion**  
The claim that "more Ukrainians had been ill with influenza than COVID-19" is partially accurate if comparing annual flu and ARVI case numbers to COVID-19 case numbers. It is true that in some years, especially before the pandemic, the number of reported influenza and ARVI cases exceeded the cumulative number of confirmed COVID-19 cases. However, differences in surveillance, diagnosis, and reporting methods complicate a direct comparison. Additionally, the impact of COVID-19 in terms of severity and public health consequences has far surpassed that of seasonal influenza. 

In summary, while the claim holds some truth numerically, it lacks important context and may be misleading without a deeper understanding of how cases are counted and the differing impact of the two diseases.

This assertion has generated concern and debate online, prompting many to question the safety profile of COVID-19 vaccines in Ukraine and whether there is a surge in adverse reactions leading to widespread medical consultations.

To evaluate this claim, it is important to understand Ukraine’s COVID-19 vaccination campaign, the reporting systems for vaccine side effects, and official data on post-vaccination adverse events.

Ukraine began its nationwide COVID-19 vaccination campaign in early 2021, utilizing vaccines such as AstraZeneca, Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna, and CoronaVac. As with other countries, Ukrainian health authorities established monitoring and reporting mechanisms for adverse events following immunization (AEFI). Healthcare providers and recipients are encouraged to report any side effects experienced after vaccination, ranging from mild symptoms like fever and arm soreness to more serious reactions.

Globally, COVID-19 vaccines have undergone extensive clinical trials and real-world surveillance, demonstrating strong safety profiles. The vast majority of side effects are mild and temporary. Serious adverse reactions are very rare and are closely monitored by health agencies.

In Ukraine, the Ministry of Health periodically publishes data on the number and type of adverse events reported after vaccination. According to publicly available figures, most reported side effects among Ukrainians have been mild, such as fever, headache, or localized pain at the injection site. While there have been reports of individuals seeking medical attention for more pronounced symptoms, the proportion of such cases remains low relative to the total number of vaccine doses administered.

The claim of a “massive” wave of Ukrainians seeking medical help post-vaccination suggests either a sudden, large-scale surge in adverse events or an unusual pattern compared to other countries. However, available data from Ukrainian health authorities does not support this characterization. Experts explain that it is routine for a small percentage of vaccine recipients to consult healthcare professionals for reassurance or to address concerns about side effects. This does not indicate an underlying crisis or a fundamental problem with vaccine safety.

Furthermore, Ukraine’s experience is consistent with global trends, where the majority of vaccine side effects are minor and self-limiting. Health authorities have emphasized that the benefits of COVID-19 vaccination far outweigh the risks of side effects, particularly given the potential severity of COVID-19 itself.

In conclusion, while some Ukrainians, like people everywhere, have sought medical help for post-vaccination symptoms, the evidence does not support the claim of a massive surge in such cases. The official data and expert analysis indicate that the incidence of adverse reactions requiring medical attention remains low and within expected parameters. The Ukrainian vaccination campaign continues with oversight and transparency, and there is no indication of an extraordinary public health concern related to vaccine safety.

article_content:
A claim has recently circulated on social media, alleging that Japan has banned blood donations from individuals who have received a COVID-19 vaccine. This assertion has raised concerns among the public and generated widespread discussion about vaccine safety and blood donation policies in Japan. A close examination of the facts, however, reveals that this claim is unfounded.

To understand the context, it is important to recognize that blood donation eligibility criteria are maintained by national health authorities and blood services, such as the Japanese Red Cross Society. The purpose of these guidelines is to ensure the safety of both blood donors and recipients. During the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines, many countries, including Japan, reviewed and updated their blood donation protocols to address questions about the new vaccines.

In Japan, people who wish to donate blood must meet certain health requirements. Regarding COVID-19 vaccination, the Japanese Red Cross Society has issued specific guidance. According to their protocols, individuals who have received an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine—such as those produced by Pfizer-BioNTech or Moderna—are generally eligible to donate blood after a short waiting period. This precautionary window, typically 48 hours, allows time to monitor for potential side effects like fever or allergic reactions, which could temporarily impact donor health. After this brief period, if the donor feels well and meets all other eligibility criteria, they may donate blood as usual.

There is no evidence to support the claim that Japan has instituted a blanket ban on blood donations from people vaccinated against COVID-19. In fact, Japanese health authorities encourage eligible individuals, including those vaccinated, to donate blood, as maintaining an adequate blood supply is essential for healthcare services. The only restrictions typically apply to those experiencing post-vaccination symptoms, or those who have received specific types of vaccines not approved in Japan, in which case the waiting period may be longer.

The spread of misinformation about blood donation policies and COVID-19 vaccination can have negative consequences. Misleading claims may deter vaccinated individuals from donating blood, potentially reducing the overall supply and affecting patients in need of transfusions. It is crucial that the public relies on official guidance from reputable sources, such as government health agencies and the Japanese Red Cross Society.

In conclusion, the assertion that Japan has banned blood donations from individuals vaccinated against COVID-19 is false. Japan permits blood donations from vaccinated individuals following a short waiting period, provided they are otherwise eligible and symptom-free. The public is encouraged to consult official channels for the most current and accurate information on blood donation policies.

A recent social media post has sparked controversy by claiming, “Ventilation equipment is artificial death.” This provocative statement raises concerns about the use of mechanical ventilation in medical care, particularly in critical care settings. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine what ventilation equipment does, when and why it is used, and the outcomes associated with its use.

Mechanical ventilation refers to the use of machines—such as ventilators—to assist or completely take over a person’s breathing when they are unable to breathe adequately on their own. This intervention is commonly used in hospitals for patients with severe respiratory failure, during surgery, or in intensive care units (ICUs) for those suffering from acute illnesses like pneumonia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbations, or during life-threatening conditions such as cardiac arrest.

The core claim in the post equates the use of ventilation equipment with causing “artificial death.” This phrase suggests that being placed on a ventilator is equivalent to hastening or ensuring a patient’s demise. However, the medical reality is far more nuanced. Ventilators are life-sustaining devices; they are designed to support patients through periods of acute illness, giving their bodies time to recover. In many cases, mechanical ventilation is a temporary measure that allows for successful treatment and eventual recovery.

Complications can arise from prolonged use of mechanical ventilation, including ventilator-associated pneumonia, lung injury, and difficulties in weaning patients off the machine. Despite these risks, the primary intention of ventilation is to save lives, not end them. Medical professionals carefully evaluate each patient’s condition to determine whether ventilation is appropriate and beneficial.

There are situations, particularly in cases of severe, irreversible illness or at the end of life, where mechanical ventilation may prolong the dying process without offering meaningful recovery. In these instances, families and clinicians may face tough decisions about withdrawing support. These ethically complex scenarios are often guided by advance directives, patient wishes, and considerations of quality of life. However, the act of providing ventilation itself is not the same as causing death. Rather, it is a medical intervention that can either support recovery or, in some cases, delay the natural process of dying.

It is important to distinguish between the goals of medical care and the tools used to achieve them. Ventilation equipment is not inherently an “artificial death”; it is a tool that can be used to sustain life. The outcome depends on the patient’s underlying health, the cause of respiratory failure, and the clinical circumstances.

In summary, the claim that “ventilation equipment is artificial death” is misleading. While mechanical ventilation cannot guarantee recovery in every case, it is a critical component of modern medicine that saves countless lives each year. Its use, risks, and limitations must be weighed carefully, but equating its application to causing death does not reflect the reality of its role in healthcare.

Em muitos casos, a ventilação mecânica é uma medida temporária que permite o tratamento bem-sucedido e a recuperação eventual.

A claim circulating on social media alleges that the COVID-19 outbreak in India is a “complete fraud.” This assertion suggests that the pandemic’s impact in India was either fabricated or exaggerated and that the crisis did not exist as reported. To assess the validity of this claim, it is necessary to examine the available evidence, the timeline of the outbreak, and the experiences of those affected.

COVID-19, caused by the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, was declared a pandemic by the World Health Organization in March 2020. Like many countries, India faced significant challenges in containing the spread of the virus. The first confirmed case in India was reported in January 2020, and the number of infections grew rapidly thereafter.

By mid-2021, India experienced one of the world’s largest COVID-19 surges. Hospitals in major cities such as Delhi, Mumbai, and Bengaluru were overwhelmed with patients. News reports, firsthand accounts, and images from the period documented shortages of hospital beds, oxygen supplies, and critical medicines. Many families shared stories of struggling to find treatment for their loved ones. Crematoriums and burial grounds in several cities reported a sharp increase in activity, with photographs and videos showing queues and mass cremations.

The government of India implemented a nationwide lockdown in March 2020 to slow the spread of the virus. Further waves of infection prompted regional restrictions, mass testing, and one of the largest vaccination campaigns in the world. The government, health authorities, and independent observers tracked daily case numbers, hospitalizations, and fatalities. These figures, while debated in terms of accuracy and undercounting, consistently indicated a significant public health crisis.

Expert analysis from epidemiologists, public health officials, and medical professionals confirmed the presence and impact of COVID-19 in India. The country’s scientific community was actively involved in sequencing virus variants, developing vaccines, and conducting clinical research on treatments. The experiences of healthcare workers, many of whom lost colleagues and family members to the virus, further reinforce the reality of the outbreak.

While there have been legitimate debates about the accuracy of official statistics, the challenges of data collection in a country as vast as India, and the adequacy of the government response, there is extensive evidence that the COVID-19 outbreak in India was real and had devastating consequences. The assertion that the outbreak was a “complete fraud” is not supported by the overwhelming documentation, data, and lived experiences from across the country.

In summary, the claim that the COVID-19 outbreak in India is a “complete fraud” is demonstrably false. The pandemic had a profound and measurable impact on the Indian population, health system, and society. Efforts to deny the reality of the crisis undermine the experiences of those affected and the work of those who responded to the emergency.

Koronavirusi SARS-CoV-2, i cili shkakton COVID-19, u deklarua si pandemë nga Organizata Botërore e Shëndetësisë në mars 2020. Si shumë vende të tjera, Indi ka përballuar lëshime të rënda në kontrollimin e përhapjes së virusit. Rasti i parë i konfirmuar në Indi u raportua në janar 2020, dhe numri i infeksioneve u rrit shpejt pas kësaj datë.

Në mes të vitit 2021, Indi përjetoi një nga përpjekjet më të mëdha të COVID-19 në botë. Spitalët në qytete të madhështu si Delhi, Mumbai dhe Bengaluru u mbushën me pacientë. Në të njëjtën kohë, shtë të diskutuar të drejtë për saktësinë e statistikave oficiale, lëshimet e të dhënave në një vend të madh si India dhe shpërndarja e përgjegjësisë së qeverisë, ka një e mjaftueshme e dëshmimit se përpjekja e COVID-19 në Indi ishte reale dhe ka pasur konsekencat e zhurave. Në mënyrë të përgjithshme, dëshmimi se përpjekja e COVID-19 në Indi është një "falsifikim të plotë" është e shqetësuar. Përpjekjet për të denoncuar realitetin e krizës përmundëson përvojat e të afikuarve dhe punën e atyre që u përgjigjën krizës së emergjencës.

A claim circulating on social media asserts that flies are capable of distributing COVID-19. This statement has generated concern and confusion, especially as individuals continue to take precautions to prevent the spread of the virus. To accurately assess this claim, it is important to examine the science behind COVID-19 transmission, the role of insects in spreading infectious diseases, and the current understanding among health experts.

COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, which primarily spreads between people through respiratory droplets. These droplets are released when an infected person coughs, sneezes, speaks, or breathes. The virus can also be transmitted by touching surfaces contaminated with the virus and then touching the face, particularly the mouth, nose, or eyes. This mode of transmission has led to widespread emphasis on mask-wearing, hand hygiene, and surface disinfection.

Flies, particularly houseflies, are known to carry and spread a variety of pathogens, including bacteria and parasites. They do this by landing on contaminated surfaces, picking up microbes on their legs and bodies, and then transferring them to food, surfaces, or people. Flies are associated with the spread of diseases such as cholera, typhoid fever, and dysentery. Given this background, it is understandable that some might speculate about their role in the transmission of COVID-19.

However, the current scientific consensus does not support the idea that flies play a significant role in spreading SARS-CoV-2. Studies on the transmission dynamics of COVID-19 have focused on human-to-human transmission via respiratory droplets and aerosols, as well as surface contamination. There is no evidence to suggest that flies can acquire the virus from contaminated surfaces and subsequently transmit it to humans in a way that leads to infection.

Health organizations have monitored a range of potential transmission pathways since the emergence of COVID-19, including the possibility of insects acting as vectors. Thus far, there have been no confirmed cases of COVID-19 being spread by flies or other insects. The virus primarily infects the respiratory tract, and its ability to survive on a fly's body long enough to cause infection in another host is highly unlikely according to current research.

It is important to distinguish between diseases that are known to be transmitted by flies and those, like COVID-19, that are not. While maintaining cleanliness and proper food handling practices is always advisable to prevent foodborne illnesses, there is no need for additional concern about flies as vectors for COVID-19.

In summary, the claim that flies are able to distribute COVID-19 is not supported by scientific evidence. The primary mode of transmission remains close contact with infected persons and contaminated surfaces. As always, public health guidelines should be followed to reduce the risk of infection, but fears of flies spreading COVID-19 are not substantiated by current research.

Ο κορονοϊός είναι προκαλείται από τον ιό SARS-CoV-2, ο οποίος εξαπλώνεται κυρίως μεταξύ των ανθρώπων μέσω αεροσπορικών τροπικών. Αυτές οι τροπικοί απελευθερώνονται όταν ένας μολυσμένος άνθρωπος κατεβάζει, καταγγέλλει, μιλά ή αναπνέει. Οι σκωλήνες, ιδιαίτερα οι σπίτια σκωλήνες, είναι γνωστές για τη μετάδοση μιας ποικιλίας παθογόνων, συμπεριλαμβανομένων βακτηρίων και παρασίτων. Μελέτες σχετικά με την δυναμική εξαπλώσεως του κορονοϊού έχουν εστιάσει στην εξαπλώσεως ανθρώπου-ανθρώπου μέσω αεροσπορικών τροπικών και αεροσπορικών τροπικών, καθώς και την χρήση επιφανειών. Δεν υπάρχει απόδειξη ότι οι σκωλήνες μπορούν να αποκτήσουν τον ιό από χρησιμοποιημένες επιφάνειες και να τον μεταφέρουν στους ανθρώπους με τρόπο που οδηγεί στην εισβολή.

Επί του παρόντος, δεν έχουν επιβεβαιωθεί περιπτώσεις εξαπλώσεως του κορονοϊού από σκωλήνες ή άλλα έντομα. Ο ιός επικρατεί κυρίως του αναπνευστικού συστήματος, και η δυνατότητα του να υπάρχει στο σώμα ενός σκωληνιού για μεγάλο χρονικό διάστημα που να οδηγήσει σε εισβολή σε άλλο υποδοχέα είναι εξαιρετικά απίθανη, σύμφωνα με την τρέχουσα έρευνα.

Είναι σημαντικό να διακρίνουμε μεταξύ νοσημάτων που είναι γνωστά να μεταφέρονται από σκωλήνες και αυτών, όπως τον κορονοϊό, που δεν το κάνουν. Αν και η διατήρηση καθαριότητας και των κατάλληλων πρακτικών για την επεξεργασία τροφίμων είναι πάντα συνιστώμενη για την πρόληψη των τροφιμικών νοσημάτων, δεν χρειάζεται να ανησυχήσουμε περισσότερο για την αντιπροσωπεία των σκωληνιών για τον κορονοϊό.

Συνοπτικά, η δήλωση ότι οι σκωλήνες είναι δυνατόν να διανέμουν τον κορονοϊό δεν υποστηρίζεται από επιστημονικές αποδείξεις. Η κύρια μορφή μετάδοσης παραμένει η έκθεση σε μολυσμένους άνθρωπους και χρησιμοποιημένες επιφάνειες. Ως πάντοτε, πρέπει να ακολουθούνται οι οδηγίες για τη δημόσια υγεία για να μειωθεί η επικίνδυνος εισβολής, αλλά οι φόβοι για την εξαπλώσεως του κορονοϊού από σκωλήνες δεν επιβεβαιώνονται από την τρέχουσα έρευνα.

Claims have circulated widely on social media suggesting that people who have received a COVID-19 vaccine can "secrete" spike proteins from the coronavirus, potentially infecting those around them. This assertion has fueled concerns about vaccine safety and interactions with unvaccinated individuals. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine how COVID-19 vaccines work, what spike proteins are, and whether there is any scientific basis for the idea of "shedding" or transmitting spike proteins to others.

COVID-19 vaccines, including the widely used mRNA vaccines and viral vector vaccines, are designed to instruct the body's cells to produce a harmless version of the spike protein found on the surface of the coronavirus. The immune system then recognizes this protein as foreign and mounts a response, preparing the body to fight off actual infection if it occurs in the future. The spike protein produced by the vaccine is not the entire virus and cannot cause COVID-19.

The term "shedding" is sometimes used in virology to describe when a live virus in a vaccine could be spread from a vaccinated person to others. However, none of the authorized COVID-19 vaccines contain live, replicating virus. The spike protein generated after vaccination is produced in small amounts, primarily at the site of the injection, and is quickly broken down by the body. There is no evidence to suggest that vaccinated individuals excrete or "secrete" spike proteins through their breath, skin, or bodily fluids in a way that could expose or harm others.

Concerns about spike protein "shedding" seem to stem from misunderstandings about how the vaccines function. mRNA from the vaccine does not linger in the body, nor does it integrate into genetic material. The spike protein itself is not infectious; it cannot cause COVID-19 or replicate. Even in the case of viral vector vaccines, the adenovirus used as a delivery system is modified so that it cannot reproduce or cause illness.

A separate but related misconception is the idea that being near vaccinated people could cause unvaccinated individuals to develop symptoms or health issues. Extensive monitoring and research have not shown evidence of such effects. Side effects reported after vaccination, such as mild fever or arm soreness, are a result of the individual's own immune response—not something that can be transferred to others.

In summary, the claim that vaccinated people "secrete" spike proteins of the coronavirus and can infect those around them is not supported by scientific evidence. COVID-19 vaccines do not contain live virus, do not cause recipients to shed or spread spike proteins in a way that could infect others, and do not pose a risk to people in proximity to those who have been vaccinated. The vaccines are a critical tool in reducing transmission of COVID-19, not a source of new infection.

Kuid kehtivaid koronavirusvaksine ei sisalda elavat, kopeerivat viirust. Vaksine toodud spetsiifiline valgu toodab väga väike kogus, peamiselt injektsioonikohta ja see on kiiresti hõivatud kehast. Ei ole teaduslikke andmeid, et vaksineeritud inimesed võivad väljaarvutada või "väljaarvutada" spetsiifilist valgu õhku, kergest, või kehaliikumisvoolu, mis saaks põhjustada teisi inimesi või kahjustada neid.

Huvi kohta spetsiifilise valgu "väljalangusest" tundub pärinud sellest, kuidas vaksine toimib. Vaksine mRNA ei jää kehale jää, ega see integreeruks genetilise koodi. Spetsiifiline valgu ise ei ole infektsioonivõimendava ja ei saa põhjustada koronavirusinfektsiooni või kopeerida. Selles juhul ka viiruse vektorvaksine, kasutatakse adenoviiruse, mis on muudetud, et see ei saaks kopeerida ega põhjustada kahjustust.

Lisaks on olemas otsene, kuid seotud vigu, et vaksineeritud inimeste lähedus võib põhjustada tulemuslikkusega suhtless unvaksineeritud inimeste sümptomeid või tervislikke probleeme. Laias ulatuses jälgimist ja uuringuid ei ole nähtud selliseid mõjusid. Vaksineerimise tagajärjed, näiteks madala kuumuse või käe kinnitamise tund, on tulemus inimese enda immuunvastusest – midagi, mis ei saa edasi anda teistele inimestele.

A social media post has circulated claiming that two infants died as a result of receiving experimental COVID-19 vaccines during clinical trials. This assertion has contributed to ongoing concerns and misinformation about vaccine safety, particularly regarding the youngest members of the population. A careful examination of the facts is necessary to assess the accuracy of this claim.

Background: COVID-19 Vaccine Trials in Infants

Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccines have played a critical role in reducing severe illness and death. Initial clinical trials focused on adults, and only gradually did studies expand to include adolescents and younger children. Trials involving infants and very young children have followed a rigorous, phased approach, with safety protocols and oversight from regulatory agencies.

The Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna vaccines, both using mRNA technology, extended studies to infants after earlier trials in older age groups demonstrated favorable safety profiles. These pediatric trials were carefully monitored, and adverse events, including serious ones, were reported and investigated as standard procedure.

Analyzing the Claim: Did Two Infants Die from Experimental COVID-19 Vaccines?

The core claim states that two infants died as a result of receiving experimental COVID-19 vaccines during clinical testing. To assess this, it is important to distinguish between deaths that occurred among trial participants and deaths caused by the vaccine itself.

Clinical trials for pediatric COVID-19 vaccines included thousands of young participants, all of whom were closely monitored. In any large clinical trial, particularly involving very young children, some adverse events, including deaths, can occur coincidentally and are not necessarily related to the intervention being studied. Each serious adverse event is reviewed by independent safety monitoring boards to determine causality.

Publicly available data and statements from regulatory agencies indicate that while there were reports of deaths among trial participants, thorough investigations concluded these were not caused by the vaccine. For example, some deaths in clinical trials have been attributed to underlying health conditions or unrelated illnesses, not to the vaccine or its administration. No credible evidence shows that infants died as a direct result of receiving a COVID-19 vaccine during clinical trials.

It is also important to note that the term “experimental” refers to the clinical trial phase, not to the safety or scientific rigor of the vaccine. All vaccines undergo extensive pre-clinical and clinical testing before being authorized for widespread use, and trials in infants adhered to strict standards.

Conclusion

The claim that two infants died from experimental COVID-19 vaccines during clinical test work is misleading. While reports of deaths in clinical trials are always taken seriously, investigations found no evidence linking any infant deaths directly to the COVID-19 vaccine. Regulatory authorities and independent safety boards continually monitor vaccine trials, and no COVID-19 vaccine has been approved for infants without robust safety data. Spreading unsubstantiated claims can contribute to vaccine hesitancy and undermine public health efforts. It remains crucial to rely on transparent, verified information when discussing vaccine safety.

A recent social media post claims that "concentration camps" for COVID-19 patients are being created in New York City. This alarming assertion has circulated online, sparking concern and confusion among residents and observers. To clarify the facts, it is important to examine the background of New York City's response to COVID-19, analyze the terminology used, and assess the veracity of the claim.

During the height of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021, New York City faced significant challenges as one of the earliest and hardest-hit urban centers in the United States. Hospitals quickly filled to capacity, prompting authorities to seek alternative solutions to house and care for those infected. Temporary field hospitals were established in locations such as the Javits Center, Central Park, and even aboard the USNS Comfort naval ship. The goal was to expand medical care capacity and reduce the risk of disease transmission in crowded emergency rooms.

Additionally, public health officials explored quarantine measures for individuals unable to safely isolate at home. Hotels and other facilities were repurposed to serve as voluntary isolation centers for people diagnosed with COVID-19, particularly those living in shared housing or homeless shelters. These facilities provided medical supervision, meals, and social support, and individuals were encouraged—but not forcibly required—to stay for the recommended isolation period.

The use of the phrase "concentration camps" in the social media post is misleading and inflammatory. Historically, concentration camps refer to locations where large numbers of people are forcibly detained under harsh conditions, often without due process or basic human rights protections. The term is most closely associated with the atrocities committed during World War II. In contrast, the COVID-19 isolation centers in New York City were not designed or operated as detention facilities. Participation was voluntary, and individuals retained their legal rights and freedoms. There are no credible reports of patients being forcibly interned or mistreated in these facilities.

Rumors and misinformation about "COVID camps" have surfaced throughout the pandemic, often fueled by fear and misunderstanding of public health measures. In reality, New York City’s approach emphasized community support and medical care rather than coercion or punishment. While some other countries implemented compulsory quarantine for travelers or those exposed to the virus, New York City did not create facilities resembling concentration camps in any form.

In summary, there is no evidence to support the claim that "concentration camps" for COVID-19 patients are being created in New York City. The city did establish temporary medical and isolation facilities to manage the public health emergency, but these were not detention centers. The use of loaded language in the social media post distorts the facts and misrepresents the intent and nature of New York City’s COVID-19 response. Residents are advised to seek information from official sources and remain vigilant against misinformation during public health crises.

article_content:
In recent years, social media platforms have become fertile ground for the spread of health-related misinformation, particularly surrounding vaccines. One claim that has circulated widely is that magnets will stick to the spot where a person received a COVID-19 vaccine, implying that the vaccine contains magnetic or metallic ingredients that remain in the body. This assertion has sparked concern and curiosity among some members of the public, prompting fact-checkers and scientists to respond.

To understand this claim, it is helpful to review the context in which COVID-19 vaccines were developed and administered. Since late 2020, several vaccines, including those using mRNA technology such as Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, as well as viral vector vaccines like AstraZeneca and Johnson & Johnson, have been deployed globally in the fight against COVID-19. These vaccines are rigorously tested and reviewed by safety agencies before public distribution. Their ingredients are publicly disclosed, and include messenger RNA, lipid nanoparticles, salts, sugars, and stabilizers, but do not list any metals or substances known to be magnetic.

The claim that a magnet will adhere to the point of vaccine injection rests on the assumption that the vaccine introduces a magnetic substance into the body. However, a review of the ingredients shows that none are metallic or magnetic. The primary components—mRNA, lipids, salts, and stabilizers—are organic or non-metallic compounds not capable of attracting magnets. Furthermore, the human body itself is not naturally magnetic, and routine injections do not cause magnetic effects.

Numerous videos and posts have appeared online showing individuals placing magnets, coins, or other small metal objects on their arms, sometimes at the site of a recent vaccination. In these demonstrations, the object appears to stick to the skin, which is then attributed to the vaccine. However, physical explanations provide a more plausible account for these observations. Human skin can be slightly tacky due to natural oils, lotions, sweat, or moisture, and small, lightweight objects may adhere temporarily due to simple surface tension or stickiness, not magnetism. In controlled scientific settings, magnets do not stick to vaccinated arms any more than to unvaccinated arms.

Experts have also pointed out that even if a vaccine contained metallic substances—which it does not—the tiny quantities used in injections would be far too small to create any noticeable magnetic effect. The amount of material in a vaccine dose is minuscule compared to what would be required for magnetism to be observable through the skin.

In summary, the claim that a magnet is attracted to the point of introduction of the COVID-19 vaccine is not supported by scientific evidence or the known composition of the vaccines. Demonstrations purporting to show magnets sticking to vaccinated arms can be explained by factors unrelated to magnetism, such as skin moisture or adhesive residues. The spread of this claim underscores the importance of critically evaluating health information and seeking guidance from credible scientific sources.

In recent days, a social media post has circulated widely, claiming that former heavyweight boxing champion Mike Tyson referred to the COVID-19 pandemic as "Plandemia" and expressed his opposition to vaccination. Given Tyson’s public profile and influence, such statements have the potential to sway public opinion on critical health issues. This article examines the veracity of these claims, providing context, background information, and a detailed fact-checking analysis.

The word "Plandemia" is a term often used by individuals who believe that the COVID-19 pandemic was planned or orchestrated rather than being a naturally occurring global health crisis. This term is commonly associated with conspiracy theories that question the origins of the virus, the motivations of governments and health organizations, and the safety and efficacy of vaccines developed in response to the virus.

Mike Tyson, known for his forthright personality both inside and outside the ring, has commented publicly on a variety of issues, including health and wellness. Tyson’s own journey of transformation and openness about personal struggles have made him a figure whose opinions attract considerable attention. However, when it comes to the COVID-19 pandemic and vaccinations, Tyson’s public statements have been sparse and primarily focused on his personal experiences, rather than broader political or conspiratorial commentary.

To assess the claim, it is important to review Tyson’s public statements, interviews, social media posts, and appearances since the onset of the pandemic. No widely reported instances exist of Tyson using the term "Plandemia" in a public forum, interview, or social media post. Major media outlets and reputable sources have not documented Tyson directly referring to the pandemic with this conspiratorial term. In addition, Tyson has not made explicit statements opposing COVID-19 vaccination in widely circulated interviews or on his verified social media accounts.

Tyson has participated in discussions about health, including on his podcast and during interviews, but his comments have generally centered on his own lifestyle changes, mental health, and personal well-being. While he has occasionally voiced skepticism about certain aspects of mainstream narratives, there is no substantive evidence that he has publicly called the pandemic "Plandemia" or campaigned against vaccination.

It is worth noting that the spread of misinformation and misattribution of quotes to celebrities is common on social media platforms. High-profile figures are often used to lend credibility to controversial opinions that they themselves may not actually hold. The claim that Tyson used the term "Plandemia" and opposed vaccination appears to be an example of such misattribution.

In conclusion, based on available public records and statements, there is no evidence to support the claim that Mike Tyson referred to the COVID-19 pandemic as "Plandemia" or expressed opposition to vaccination. The social media post in question does not accurately reflect Tyson’s documented public statements, and the core claim remains unsubstantiated. As with all information on social media, it is essential to verify claims through reliable sources before accepting them as fact.

A claim circulating on social media asserts that COVID-19 vaccination poses particular dangers to individuals during puberty. This statement has sparked concern among parents and guardians about the safety of vaccinating adolescents. To assess the validity of this claim, it is essential to review scientific evidence, guidance from health authorities, and what is known about the effects of COVID-19 vaccines in young people undergoing puberty.

**Background on COVID-19 Vaccination in Adolescents**

COVID-19 vaccines, including mRNA vaccines such as those produced by Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, were initially authorized for adults. As data on safety and efficacy in younger age groups became available, regulatory agencies in many countries extended emergency use authorization to adolescents, typically starting at age 12. This extension followed clinical trials specifically conducted in these age groups.

Puberty is a period of rapid physical and hormonal change, typically occurring between ages 10 and 16. During puberty, the body undergoes significant development, including growth spurts and changes in sexual maturation. Concerns have been raised in some quarters about how vaccines, including COVID-19 vaccines, might interact with these developmental processes.

**Evaluating the Core Claim**

The central claim is that COVID-19 vaccination is "especially dangerous" during puberty. Scientific evidence to date does not support this assertion. Clinical trials for COVID-19 vaccines included adolescents who were in various stages of puberty. These studies monitored participants for adverse effects, both common and rare, for weeks to months following vaccination.

The most common side effects observed in adolescents mirrored those seen in adults: soreness at the injection site, mild fever, fatigue, and headaches, which generally resolved within a few days. These are typical immune responses and do not indicate heightened risk specifically linked to puberty.

A rare side effect, myocarditis (inflammation of the heart muscle), was identified primarily in male adolescents and young adults following mRNA vaccination. However, cases were generally mild, resolved quickly, and occurred at a much lower rate than heart complications seen in adolescents who contracted COVID-19 itself. Major health organizations have reviewed these findings and continue to recommend COVID-19 vaccination for eligible adolescents, as the benefits in preventing severe illness and complications from COVID-19 outweigh the risks.

To date, there is no credible scientific evidence indicating that COVID-19 vaccines interfere with puberty-related hormonal changes, growth, or development. No increase in adverse events unique to puberty has been observed in vaccination safety monitoring systems.

**Conclusion**

The claim that COVID-19 vaccination is especially dangerous during puberty is not supported by current scientific evidence or the consensus of major health organizations. While, as with any vaccination, there are potential side effects, the risks for adolescents—including those going through puberty—are low and generally outweighed by the benefits of protection against COVID-19. Parents and guardians concerned about vaccination during puberty are encouraged to consult with healthcare providers, who can provide individualized guidance based on the latest evidence.

A claim circulating on social media asserts that the effectiveness rate of the COVID-19 vaccine is just 1%. This statement suggests that the vaccine offers minimal protection against the virus, raising concerns among the public about its utility and impact. In this article, we examine the accuracy of this claim by providing context on vaccine effectiveness, reviewing relevant scientific data, and analyzing how such figures are calculated and interpreted.

To begin, understanding how vaccine effectiveness is measured is crucial. Vaccine effectiveness refers to the percentage reduction in disease among vaccinated individuals compared to those who are unvaccinated, under real-world conditions. This figure is typically calculated after large-scale clinical trials and ongoing surveillance post-authorization, and it reflects the vaccine’s ability to prevent infections, severe illness, hospitalizations, and deaths.

The claim that COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness is only 1% starkly contrasts with initial findings from large clinical trials. When the first COVID-19 vaccines were authorized, studies found effectiveness rates ranging from roughly 70% to 95% in preventing symptomatic COVID-19 infection. These percentages represented a substantial reduction in risk for those who received the vaccine compared to those who did not. For example, if 100 out of 1,000 unvaccinated people contracted COVID-19, a 95% effective vaccine would mean only 5 out of 1,000 vaccinated people would contract the virus under similar exposure conditions.

Over time, with the emergence of new variants and waning immunity, effectiveness against infection has decreased somewhat, though vaccines continue to provide strong protection against severe disease, hospitalization, and death. Booster doses have been shown to restore or enhance this protection. Public health agencies have continued to monitor effectiveness, and while protection against mild or asymptomatic infection may be reduced, the prevention of severe outcomes remains significant.

The origin of the 1% effectiveness figure appears to stem from a misunderstanding of absolute risk reduction versus relative risk reduction. Relative risk reduction, commonly reported in clinical trials, refers to the proportional decrease in disease risk (e.g., 95%), while absolute risk reduction refers to the difference in the actual rates of infection between vaccinated and unvaccinated groups, which can be much smaller if the overall risk in the population is low. Some critics have used the lower absolute risk reduction to argue that vaccine efficacy is minimal, but this interpretation can be misleading. Absolute risk reduction depends heavily on the baseline risk in the population and does not negate the substantial reduction in risk for individuals or the population-level benefits of vaccination.

In summary, the claim that the COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness rate is 1% does not accurately reflect the evidence from clinical trials or real-world data. COVID-19 vaccines have demonstrated much higher effectiveness rates, especially against severe disease and death. Misinterpretations of statistical measures may contribute to confusion, but the consensus among health experts remains clear: COVID-19 vaccines offer important protection and have played a crucial role in reducing the impact of the pandemic.

A recent social media post claims that the COVID-19 vaccine killed more than 10,000 Europeans in a span of four months. This claim has circulated widely, fueling ongoing debates about vaccine safety. To assess its accuracy, it is crucial to analyze available data, understand vaccine surveillance systems, and consider the broader context of the pandemic and vaccination campaigns.

COVID-19 vaccines were introduced in Europe in late 2020 and early 2021, with massive rollouts coordinated by national governments and the European Medicines Agency (EMA). The primary vaccines authorized included Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna, AstraZeneca, and Johnson & Johnson, each subject to rigorous clinical trials and continuous safety monitoring. As of mid-2021, hundreds of millions of vaccine doses had been administered across the continent.

Central to vaccine monitoring are adverse event reporting systems such as EudraVigilance, which collects reports of potential side effects following vaccination. These systems are designed to identify rare risks that may not have emerged during trials. However, it is important to distinguish between reported deaths and deaths causally linked to vaccines. When individuals die after vaccination, these events are reported for investigation, but not all are found to be caused by the vaccine itself. Many reported deaths are coincidental, related to underlying health conditions or other factors.

Claims that more than 10,000 Europeans died from the COVID-19 vaccine in four months typically stem from misinterpretations of adverse event database entries. For example, EudraVigilance might record thousands of deaths reported after vaccination; however, these numbers do not reflect deaths proven to have been caused by the vaccine. Regulatory authorities review each case to assess causality. The vast majority of deaths reported are found to be unrelated to vaccination, and confirmed deaths directly caused by the vaccine are exceedingly rare.

The EMA and national health agencies have acknowledged that, like any medical intervention, COVID-19 vaccines can have side effects, including rare but serious adverse reactions. However, the risk of severe outcomes from COVID-19 itself far outweighs the risks associated with vaccination. The benefit-risk assessment strongly favors vaccination, especially among vulnerable populations.

In summary, there is no credible evidence to support the claim that COVID-19 vaccines killed more than 10,000 Europeans in four months. The figure appears to be a misrepresentation of raw reports from surveillance systems, which do not equate to confirmed vaccine-related deaths. Expert reviews and ongoing safety monitoring have consistently shown that serious adverse events are rare and that the vaccines provide substantial protection against COVID-19. Public health authorities continue to recommend vaccination as a critical tool in controlling the pandemic.

વેક્સીન મૂલ્યાંકનની કેન્દ્રિત પ્રણાલીઓ જેમ કે ઇયુડ્રાવિગિલન્સ એવી અસ્થિરતા ઘટનાઓની રિપોર્ટિંગ પ્રણાલીઓ છે જે વેક્સીન પછી સંભાવિત પરિણામોની રિપોર્ટ સંગ્રહ કરે છે. આ પ્રણાલીઓ કસોટીઓ દરમિયાન પ્રગટ થયેલી નાની જોખમોની ઓળખ માટે ડિઝાઇન કરવામાં આવી છે. તેથી, વેક્સીન પછી મૃત્યુની રિપોર્ટ અને વેક્સીન સાથે કારણ સંબંધિત મૃત્યુની વચ્ચે વિભેદન કરવો મહત્વપૂર્ણ છે. જ્યારે વેક્સીન પછી મૃત્યુ થાય છે ત્યારે તેનો અભ્યાસ માટે રિપોર્ટ કરવામાં આવે છે, પરંતુ તમામ મૃત્યુઓનો વેક્સીન સાથેના સંબંધ સ્થાપિત થતો નથી. અનેક રિપોર્ટ કરવામાં આવેલા મૃત્યુઓ સામાન્ય રીતે અન્ય આશ્ચર્ય જાણીતા સ્વાસ્થ્ય સ્થિતિઓ અથવા અન્ય કારણો સાથે સંબંધિત છે.

બે હજાર યુરોપિયનોની મૃત્યુ વેક્સીન કારણે થયેલા હોવાનો દાવો મુખ્યત્વે અસ્થિરતા ડેટાબેઝ નોંધોના ખોટા અંદાજનના કારણે થયો છે. ઉદાહરણ તરીકે, ઇયુડ્રાવિગિલન્સ વેક્સીન પછી મૃત્યુઓની સેન્સર કરી શકે છે જેનો કોઈપણ સંખ્યા વેક્સીનથી કારણે થયેલા મૃત્યુઓની પુષ્ટિ કરતી નથી. નિયમનાત્મક અધિકારીઓ દરેક કેસનો કારણ મૂલ્યાંકન કરે છે. મૃત્યુઓની મોટાભાગની રિપોર્ટ વેક્સીન સાથે સંબંધિત નથી, અને વેક્સીનથી સીધો કારણે થયેલા મૃત્યુઓની સંખ્યા અત્યંત નાની છે.

ઇએમએ અને રાષ્ટ્રીય સ્વાસ્થ્ય એજન્સીઓએ જણાવ્યું છે કે, કોવિડ-19 વેક્સીન કોઈપણ ચિકિત્સા સાધન જેવું હોઈ શકે છે, જેની પાસે પ્રભાવો હોઈ શકે છે, જેમાં નાની પણ ગંભીર અસ્થિરતા પ્રતિક્રિયાઓ શામેલ છે. પરંતુ કોવિડ-19 પોતે મૃત્યુની ખૂબ જ ઊંચી સંભાવના છે, જે વેક્સીનની સાથેની ખતરનાકતાઓ કરતાં વધુ છે. ફાયદો-ખતરો મૂલ્યાંકન વેક્સીન માટે ખૂબ જ મૂલ્યવાન છે, ખાસ કરીને સ્વલ્પ સંવેદનશીલ વર્ગના લોકોમાં.

સારાંશ તરીકે, કોવિડ-19 વેક્સીનના કારણે ચાર મહિનામાં લાખો યુરોપિયનોની મૃત્યુ થયેલી હોવાનો કોઈપણ વાસ્તવિક સાક્ષ્ય નથી. આ સંખ્યા સુરક્ષા પ્રણાલીઓના મૂળ રિપોર્ટની ખોટી વ્યાખ્યાના પરિણામ છે, જે વેક્સીન સાથેના સંબંધિત મૃત્યુઓની પુષ્ટિ કરતી નથી. વિશેષજ્ઞોની મૂલ્યાંકન અને સતત સુરક્ષા મૂલ્યાંકન માટે સીધો વિસ્તાર વિસ્તરણ અત્યંત નાનો છે અને વેક્સીનો કોવિડ-19 સામે સુસ્ત રક્ષણ પૂરું પાડે છે. સામાજિક સ્વાસ્થ્ય અધિકારીઓ પ્રાથમિકતાની જરૂરિયાત તરીકે વેક્સીનેશનની સૂચના ચાલુ રાખે છે.
